PTAssess your Revenue System

CRM · Agents · Context · 13 min read

The CRM is no longer only the System of Record. It is becoming the Context System for agents.

A CRM can contain the right data and still fail to answer the question an agent needs in order to act. In an agentic operating model, data quality is necessary but not sufficient: usable context becomes a production dependency.

RevOpsHubs analysis · 4 October 2026

For years, the core CRM question was relatively simple: do we have the right data in the system?

Agents change the question.

An agent does not only need to know that a contact, company or deal exists. It needs to understand who it is, how it relates to the rest of the system, its current state, what happened before, what seems to be happening next, which rules apply and what the agent is allowed to do.

That is context.

RevOpsHubs Thesis

The CRM remains the System of Record. But for agents it is also becoming a Context System: the layer that turns distributed data into a sufficiently coherent representation of the business to support a decision.

Data is not context

Picture a deal with 80 correctly populated properties.

An agent receives one instruction: “decide the next best action.”

Amount, close date, pipeline and owner may not be enough. The agent may also need to know:

  • who the decision maker is and who is only a user;
  • whether the main contact is still engaged;
  • what each side committed to in the last conversation;
  • whether another deal is open for the same account;
  • why the opportunity is actually stalled;
  • which observable criteria allow movement to the next stage;
  • whether it can only recommend an action or execute it.

The data may already exist. The question is whether it is associated correctly, current, semantically stable and available in a form that is useful for that decision.

This is why Semantic Debt and context readiness are different problems. Semantic Debt asks whether information has stable meaning. Context readiness asks whether the agent has the right combination of information for a specific job.

The Agent Context Stack

RevOpsHubs uses seven layers to test whether an agent has enough operating context.

01

Identity — what entity is this?

Contact, company, deal, ticket or another object. Can the agent identify the right entity, detect meaningful duplicates and understand which records represent the same real-world thing?

02

Relationship — how is it connected?

Associations, buying-committee role, parent company, territory, owner, related deals, products and relationships between people. An isolated record rarely carries enough context.

03

State — where is it now?

Lifecycle, sales stage, onboarding state, risk, renewal, SLA or another current operating state. The agent needs an authoritative view of the present.

04

History — what happened before?

Emails, meetings, stage changes, tasks, notes, proposals and prior commitments. Without history, an agent can make a logically correct but operationally absurd recommendation.

05

Intent — what appears to be happening next?

Goals, urgency, objections, interest, risks and likely next step. This is where observed facts must be separated from inference. Intent can be useful without being treated as absolute truth.

06

Rules — which rules apply?

ICP, qualification, stage criteria, pricing, discount policy, SLAs, territory rules, hand-offs and exceptions. Without rules, the agent has descriptive context but not operating context.

07

Permissions — what may it actually do?

Which data it can read, which fields it can write, which messages it may send, which actions require approval and when it must escalate to a person.

Together, these seven layers form the Agent Context Stack.

An agent does not need “more data”. It needs enough context for the decision we are asking it to make.

Why this matters now

Agents can already combine multiple sources of context and take action.

Evidence
HubSpot's public Agent Builder documentation lets teams define runtime inputs, persistent knowledge, CRM read/write access and external MCP actions. HubSpot itself uses examples where agents combine deal details, associated company information and recent activity to analyse onboarding.

In ChatGPT, MCP apps can also move beyond search and reading into write and modify actions, with workspace controls and access governance.

The shift is architectural, not merely technical: once an agent can read across systems and act, context quality becomes a production dependency.

Example: inbound qualification

Imagine an agent that receives inbound leads and recommends whether they should go to SDR, nurture or disqualification.

A shallow implementation may provide title, company, employee count, source and pages visited.

A Context Stack implementation asks more:

  • Identity: do this contact and company already exist? Are there duplicates or strategic accounts?
  • Relationship: is there an open deal, customer relationship or existing owner?
  • State: where are they in the lifecycle and sales process now?
  • History: have there been prior meetings, lost deals or requests?
  • Intent: does behaviour indicate early research or an explicit need?
  • Rules: what are the current ICP and sales-acceptance criteria?
  • Permissions: may the agent only recommend, or also update Lifecycle Stage, assign an owner and create tasks?

The same model applies to meeting preparation, next-best-action, onboarding, support and renewal.

Five failures that look like AI problems but are context problems

Association

The right data is on the wrong record

The contact data is valid, but the contact is attached to the wrong company or multiple deals without a clear role.

Recency

The state is stale

The agent treats “Open deal” as current reality even though the process moved elsewhere.

Semantics

The meaning is unstable

“Qualified” means different things to different teams. Automation scales a human ambiguity.

Inference

Intent is treated as fact

A probabilistic signal starts driving action without confidence levels or validation.

Authority

The agent does not know which rule wins

CRM, spreadsheet and internal documentation disagree. There is no source of truth or precedence rule.

Permission

Context is confused with autonomy

Because the agent can infer the next step, the design assumes it may also execute it.

Design context by use case

We do not recommend building one universal “mega context” for every agent.

That increases cost, noise, excessive permissions and evaluation difficulty.

For each use case, define a minimum Context Contract:

  1. which entity starts the work;
  2. which relationships are mandatory;
  3. which state must be current;
  4. which history window matters;
  5. which intent signals may be used and at what confidence;
  6. which rules are authoritative;
  7. which permissions and approvals constrain execution.

This connects directly to the Agent Operating Contract. The Operating Contract governs the agent. The Context Contract governs the minimum information the agent needs in order to work.

Test context before testing the prompt

A great prompt cannot compensate for broken relationships, stale states or contradictory rules.

Before production, choose one use case and test the seven layers.

The next CRM project is not only about data

For a long time, improving the CRM meant collecting more data, cleaning properties and increasing adoption.

That work remains necessary.

But as agents enter the Revenue System, a new requirement appears: the system must represent operating context clearly enough for software to make a decision without inventing what is missing.

That is why the CRM is becoming more than a System of Record.

It is becoming the Context System where humans, workflows and agents learn what is actually happening in the business.
